walkthroughs.body_html:
Economic Activity & Energy — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Economic Activity & Energy brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Economic Activity & Energy.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a primary sector activity?
options: Fishing
Car manufacturing
Banking
Software research

mcqs.q: As a country industrialises, employment typically:
options: Shifts from the primary sector into secondary and tertiary work
Shifts from services back into farming
Stays exactly the same
Moves entirely into the quaternary sector immediately
Natural gas
Wind
Solar
Tidal

mcqs.q: The informal sector is best described as:
options: Unregulated work outside official records, such as street trading
Government employment
Factory work with formal contracts
Jobs in scientific research

mcqs.q: Does a falling share of factory jobs mean a country's manufacturing has collapsed?
options: Factory jobs disappear because factories close every winter.
Not necessarily — mechanisation lets output rise while employment falls, and the share can also drop simply because services are growing faster.
Nuclear power is generated from recycled batteries.
Fewer manufacturing workers always means less manufacturing output.

mcqs.q: Is the informal sector simply a problem to be eliminated?
options: The informal sector means people working in casual clothes.
Informal work has no value to a city's economy.
Nuclear power is generated from recycled batteries.
It avoids taxes and worker protections, but it also provides vital incomes, goods and services where formal jobs are scarce, so cities usually aim to manage and gradually formalise it.
Because nuclear power is low-carbon it must be renewable.
Factory jobs disappear because factories close every winter.
Nuclear power is generated from recycled batteries.
No — it is low-carbon but relies on finite uranium, so it is classed as non-renewable; renewability and carbon emissions are different ideas.
